To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) previous influenza virus infection protects from subsequent respiratory syncytial (RSV) virus–induced immunopathology, 2) this protection is due to the induction of regulatory T cells (Tregs), 3) this protection is long lasting, and 4) it is mediated by the attachment protein (G) of RSV.
influenza virus infection of the lung in mice protects from RSV-induced immunopathology.
Previous lung infections can protect against the immunopathology of subsequent infections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the innate immune system in the pathogenesis of respiratory viral infections, and the effect of infection history in this process.

the role of previous infection with influenza virus in the response to subsequent infection with respiratory syncytial (RSV) virus, which can cause severe respiratory disease in young children and adults with chronic respiratory disease.
how previous infection affects susceptibility to a subsequent challenge.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the data suggest that previous lung infection with influenza virus protects against the immunopathological effects of subsequent RSV infection.
influenza virus infection of lungs of mice protects against respiratory syncytial (RSV)–induced immunopathology.
influenza virus infection protects mice from RSV-induced immunopathology, which may have important implications for humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
influenza virus infection can protect from the immunopathological effects of RSV infection.
influenza virus infection of the respiratory tract can protect against RSV-induced immunopathology, but not viral replication.
prior influenza virus lung infection protects from respiratory syncytial viral (RSV) immunopathology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
infection history matters and can be protective.
prior infection with a virus can protect from the effects of a second virus infection.
the immune system is not a clean slate, but is primed by prior infections, and this can have a major impact on how the immune system responds to subsequent infections and vaccines.
